implementation_notes: The JDK's own plugin mechanism: the host calls ServiceLoader.load(Codec.class) and the loader reads provider-configuration files named after the service type in META-INF/services on the class path or module path, instantiating the listed classes with their public no-argument constructor. Providers are found lazily and cached, stream() exposes ServiceLoader.Provider objects so a host can filter on the provider type before instantiating anything, and reload() clears the cache; a new provider is simply another JAR, so the host is never recompiled. The plugin factory from the classic pattern collapses into the loader plus the zero-argument constructor, and a static provider() method can even hand construction to a factory.
pitfalls: ServiceLoader.load uses the current thread's context class loader (or the caller's), so a host that runs under a different class loader - plugin container, application server, custom loader - silently finds no providers.

Providers are cached per loader instance and per class loader JVM-wide advice aside, so new JARs are invisible until reload() or a new loader; and ServiceConfigurationError is thrown lazily from the iterator, far from the load call.

variants.name: JPMS module declarations (provides/uses) and module layers
variants.implementation_notes: With the module system the provider file disappears: a provider module declares provides com.example.Codec with com.example.csv.CsvCodec in module-info, the host module declares uses com.example.Codec (and requires the module that exports the service), and the host may load providers from a specific ModuleLayer - which is how a running JVM can host a plugin installed or replaced after start-up. Because the declaration is compiled into the module descriptor, the compiler and jlink can see the wiring, and the host no longer needs to require the provider modules themselves.
pitfalls: A module-installed provider must be accessible to the loader that starts the lookup; mixing class-path providers with named-module providers means the module one is ignored when the same provider class is also listed in a services file.

Module layers are not unloadable in practice once classes are resolved; hot removal requires discarding the whole layer and any code that still references its types, which is stricter than the class-path case.
